instrucciones:
Recibes registros de una base de reglas de producción audiovisual con IA (texto completo, puede estar en
inglés, ruso o español). Para CADA registro devuelve:
- "enunciado": la regla en español, UNA frase, sin adornos: qué exige, prohíbe, limita o especifica. Si el registro
  es un ejemplo o una explicación sin norma, di qué ilustra ("Ejemplo: ...", "Explicación: ...").
- "alcance": a qué aplica exactamente (modelo y versión, caso T1-T5, etapa, tipo de pieza, régimen) o "general".
- "temas": de 1 a 3 claves de la lista, las que mejor describen de qué trata la regla.
Lista de temas (clave: descripción):
marca_brandlock: brand-lock: secciones, paleta hex, tipografía, never list, voz, confianza de valores
estrategia_conceptos: brief, SMP, territorios, concept cards, matriz, dirección narrativa
guion_formato: guion: sluglines, acción, personajes, diálogo, XML, estructura, escenas
dramaturgia_escena: fórmula de escena, three-jobs, blocking, staging, poder, geometría, mirada
tres_detalles: ley de los tres detalles: presión ambiental, micro-acción, motivo sonoro/visual
emocion_sin_nombrar: mostrar no contar, emoción como cuerpo u objeto, 2-4 señales
vocabulario_prohibido: palabras vetadas, anti-slop, cinematic/epic/masterpiece, adjetivos vacíos
cinco_anclas_motivo: cinco anclas, objeto ancla, motivo, imagen final, quiebre
ritmo_montaje: ritmo, densidad de cortes, escalera, pausa, Murch, transiciones, cut types
funcion_de_plano: etiquetas Establish/Power/Pressure/Detail/..., captions de carrera, beats
beat_framework_timing: frameworks de beats, duración de shots, hook, CTA, curva de energía
shots_json_schema: shots.json, campos, schema, series_lock, rationale, run.json, versión
texto_en_pantalla: texto/overlays/tipografía en pantalla, text-overlays.json, nunca en el prompt, lectura
logos_marcas_en_imagen: logos, lettering, marcas generadas, patrocinadores, composición en post
consistencia_identidad: identidad de personaje, bloque de identidad, maestros, verbatim, clones, drift
referencias_roles: imágenes de referencia, @img, elements, ingredients, rol de cada referencia, límites de refs
genesis_maestros: génesis sin refs, T1 rostro, T2 cuerpo, placa vacía, canonizar, dos pasos
composicion_insercion: cuadros con varios sujetos, inserción secuencial, anclas de posición, contacto, manos
edicion_imagen: edición quirúrgica, preserve list, un cambio por iteración, edit no re-roll, inpainting
estructura_prompt_imagen: slots/secciones del prompt de imagen, orden, 5 slots, prosa NB, metadatos fuera
estructura_prompt_video: esqueletos de prompt de video por modelo, bloques, orden, peso al inicio
longitud_prompt: número de palabras, elementos máximos, compresión, presupuesto
negativos: negative prompt, no X, framing positivo, prohibiciones en el prompt
parametros_tecnicos: aspect ratio, resolución, duración, seed, quality, cfg, flags, parámetros API
seleccion_modelo: qué modelo usar para qué, ruteo, cuándo escalar, costos por modelo
capacidades_modelo: límites y capacidades de cada modelo, versiones, fallos conocidos del modelo
camara_movimiento: movimiento de cámara, uno por shot, motivado, vocabulario de movimientos, rig montable
encuadre_lente_dof: encuadre ECU-EWS, lente mm, profundidad de campo, compresión
angulo_camara: ángulo y altura de cámara, low/high/dutch/overhead, poder
composicion_frame: tercios, espacio negativo, capas FG/MG/BG, simetría, punto focal, dónde va el cuerpo
luz: fuente motivada, dirección, dureza, contraluz, specular, 70% sin luz, prácticos
color_grade_paleta: paleta concreta, grade, stock de película, textura, grano, halación, HDR
piel_rostro_realismo: piel, poros, look plástico, rostros, anti-AI look, realismo fotográfico
anatomia_manos: manos, dedos, anatomía, lateralidad, inspección al 100%
movimiento_congelado_blur: still como instante congelado, blur diferencial, cues de movimiento, estado posterior
fisica_consecuencia: física por consecuencia, agua, spray, humo, partículas, deformación
velocidad_vehiculo: cues de velocidad, rim barrido, carreras, vehículos, anti-fake
multitud_grupo: multitud anónima, ensamble, número de personas, rostros legibles
clima_atmosfera: lluvia, niebla, rayo, polvo, presión ambiental, una sola atmósfera
audio_dialogo: audio, diálogo, lip-sync, SFX, música, VO, marcadores de audio
continuidad_multiclip: continuidad entre clips, repetir bloque, luz constante, empalme de clips
multishot: varios shots en una generación, marcadores de corte, anti-mush
i2v_keyframes: imagen a video, primer/último frame, no re-describir, motion brief
edicion_extension_video: editar video existente, extender, ultra long, blockout, green screen
critica_qa: crítica por capas, severidad, verdict, ACCEPT/REVISE/REJECT, re-roll vs post
revision_iteracion: revisión selectiva, rondas, máximo de intentos, cambio de método, costo
validacion_gates: validadores, linter, gates, micro-gate, pregunta de avance, checks mecánicos
trazabilidad_procedencia: hashes, snapshot, run.json, rondas, procedencia, fuente de verdad
entrega_paquete: production package, preview HTML, estructura de carpetas, atribución, checklist
postproduccion: edición, grade, audio en post, export, specs de plataforma
patrones_genero: plantillas por género: moda, comida, producto, retrato, póster, UI, social
layout_grafico: slides, infografías, grids, multi-panel, bento, layouts
animacion_ilustracion: animación, principios Disney, estilos ilustrados, anime, 3D
conducta_agente: cómo responde y trabaja el agente: leer skills, preguntar, formato de respuesta, no inventar
flujo_pipeline: tracks, etapas, orden, sub-skills, carga de skills, gates entre etapas
regimenes_etiquetado: etiquetas FUENTE/A PRUEBA/CAMPO/CANONICA, investigación de campo, esqueleto de régimen
herramientas_codigo: instalación, uso y mantenimiento de herramientas, scripts, CI
ejemplo_marca: contenido de una marca o proyecto de ejemplo concreto (WhyStrohm, Acme, café, etc.)
Devuelve JSON {"registros": [{"id": "...", "enunciado": "...", "alcance": "...", "temas": ["..."]}]} con
exactamente los ids recibidos, en el mismo orden.

registros.texto: [Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Syntax pattern] Comma-separated phrases. No full sentences. No connective words ("the", "with", "and") unless they're load-bearing.
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--ar` · Values: aspect ratio · Default to use: from `project.aspect` · Notes: `--ar 9:16`, `--ar 16:9`, `--ar 1:1`

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--style` · Values: `raw` / `4a` / `4b` / `4c` · Default to use: `raw` · Notes: `raw` for photorealistic, omit for default Midjourney aesthetic

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--s` · Values: 0–1000 · Default to use: `50` for branded, `250` for artistic · Notes: Stylization weight. Lower = closer to prompt, higher = more MJ aesthetic
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--c` · Values: 0–100 · Default to use: omit · Notes: Chaos. Use only when exploring variations

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--seed` · Values: integer · Default to use: omit unless reproducing · Notes: For series consistency, set per-storyboard

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--cref` · Values: image URL · Default to use: use when character anchor exists · Notes: Character reference. Pair with `--cw`

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--cw` · Values: 0–100 · Default to use: `50` · Notes: Character weight. 100 = strict character match, 0 = clothing only
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Parameter reference (current as of Q2 2026)] Param: `--sref` · Values: image URL · Default to use: use when style anchor exists · Notes: Style reference
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Length] Aim for **40–80 words per prompt** including parameters. Anything over 100 words underperforms.
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] Translate shot grammar into Midjourney-friendly phrases:
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `MCU eye-level` · Midjourney phrase: `medium close-up, eye level`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `WS overhead` · Midjourney phrase: `wide shot, overhead view, top-down`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `static` · Midjourney phrase: (omit, static is default)
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `push` · Midjourney phrase: `dolly in, pushing forward`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `handheld` · Midjourney phrase: `handheld documentary feel, slight motion blur`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `shallow DOF` · Midjourney phrase: `shallow depth of field, f/1.8, bokeh background`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition mapping] shot_grammar: `deep DOF` · Midjourney phrase: `deep focus, everything sharp, f/8`

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Lighting language] Midjourney rewards specific lighting vocabulary:
- `soft natural light, large window left, warm afternoon golden hour`
- `hard top-light, single key, deep shadows, studio black backdrop`
- `practical mixed sources, neon accents, urban night, atmospheric haze`
- `volumetric backlight, rim light separating subject, cinematic haze`
- `chiaroscuro, dramatic side-light, painterly`
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Lighting language] Pull verbatim from `series_lock.lighting`.

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Composition pattern] {framing} of {subject character_anchor}, {action}, {compositional note}, {environment from series_lock}, {lighting from series_lock}, {color_grade}, cinematic photography, {brand mood adjectives} --ar {aspect} --style raw --s 50

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Example] **Shot data:**
{
  "id": "shot_03",
  "framing": "MS",
  "angle": "eye-level",
  "motion": "static",
  "subject": "Founder mid-thirties, leaning forward at laptop, face partially turned to window",
  "rationale": "MS framing leaves negative space right for text overlay"
}

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Example] **Series lock:**
character: founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck
environment: minimalist home office, white walls, oak desk
lighting: soft natural side-light, large window left, warm afternoon
color_grade: warm filmic, muted teal shadows

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Example] **Brand lock palette:** `#0F1F3A navy`, `#F5F0E8 cream`, `#D94F3A coral`
**Brand mood:** `calm, considered, operator, not creator`
**Output prompt:**
medium shot of founder mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, leaning forward at laptop, face partially turned to window light, negative space right of frame, minimalist home office, white walls, oak desk, soft natural side-light large window left, warm afternoon golden hour, warm filmic color grade, muted teal shadows, cinematic photography, calm considered operator mood --ar 9:16 --style raw --s 50
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't use "AI" or "rendered"**, produces stylized outputs that look generated
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't over-stack adjectives**, three adjectives per noun phrase max
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't include text content**, even if the shot has `on_screen_text`, leave it out. Composited separately.
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't use `--c` for series work**, chaos kills consistency
[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't change `--seed` mid-storyboard**, set once at series_lock level

[Adapter: Midjourney (v7) › API access note] Midjourney still has limited API access as of Q2 2026. For programmatic workflows, the prompts in `midjourney.txt` are designed to be pasted into Discord or the web UI. Some teams use third-party wrappers (PiAPI, Useapi.net), those generally accept the same prompt syntax.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image)] Google's Nano Banana model (`gemini-2.5-flash-image`) is the edit-and-iterate champion. Where other generators are best for first-frame creation, Nano Banana excels at variations, inpainting, and reference-based modification. The 2026 production pattern is to generate hero frames in Midjourney or Flux, then use Nano Banana for variants.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image)] For storyboard work, Nano Banana is the right choice when you need **many variations of a single concept** or you're feeding generated images back through for refinement.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Syntax pattern] Nano Banana takes natural-language prompts plus optional reference images. For text-to-image:
{Subject and action}. {Environment and lighting}. {Photographic specs and mood}.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Syntax pattern] For image-to-image (the strength), the prompt describes the modification:
{Modification description}. Keep {what to preserve}. Change {what to vary}.
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Parameters] Nano Banana goes through the Gemini API:
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Parameters] Parameter: `model` · Default: `gemini-2.5-flash-image`
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Parameters] Parameter: `aspectRatio` · Default: from `project.aspect` · Notes: Native support for `9:16`, `16:9`, `1:1`, `4:5`, `3:4`, `21:9`
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Parameters] Parameter: `numberOfImages` · Default: `1` for series, `4` for variant exploration
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Parameters] Parameter: `referenceImages` · Default: array of base64 images · Notes: Optional
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Length] Nano Banana handles **60–120 words** efficiently. Shorter than GPT Image, longer than Midjourney.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Composition pattern (text-to-image)] {Framing and subject sentence with character anchor}. {Environment and lighting from series_lock}. {Photographic spec, lens, depth of field, mood}. {Brand color grade closing}.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Composition pattern (image-to-image, the strength)] When refining a hero shot generated elsewhere:
Reference: {description of input image}. Modify the image to {specific change}. Preserve the character's {face/clothing/pose}, the {environment elements}, and the lighting direction. Change {specific element} to {target state}.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Example (text-to-image)] **Output prompt:**
Medium shot of a founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck sweater, leaning forward at his laptop with face turned partially toward window light. Composition leaves negative space on the right side. Minimalist home office, white walls, oak desk. Soft natural side-light from large window left, warm afternoon golden hour. Shot on 50mm prime, f/2.0, shallow depth of field, warm filmic color grade with muted teal shadows. Calm, considered, operator mood.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Example (image-to-image variant)] **Use case:** generated `shot_03` in Flux, want a variant where the founder is looking directly at camera
**Output prompt:**
Reference: medium shot of founder at laptop in home office, leaning forward, face partially turned to window. Modify the image so the founder looks directly into the camera lens with a calm, neutral expression. Preserve the character's face, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, body posture, the home office environment, the desk and laptop, and the warm afternoon side-lighting. Change only the head angle and gaze direction.

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Variant-generation workflow] The pattern Nano Banana enables, and the reason it's worth including in storyboard work:
1. Generate hero shot in Midjourney or Flux (one prompt → one image)
2. Feed that image to Nano Banana with variation prompts
3. Get 4–8 variants of the same shot for editorial selection
4. Composite text on the chosen variant

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Variant-generation workflow] When generating prompts for Nano Banana in `nano-banana.txt`, include both:
- The text-to-image prompt (for first-pass generation)
- A modification template comment showing how to use the result for variants:

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Variant-generation workflow] # shot_01, text-to-image prompt:
{prompt}

# shot_01, variant template (after generating once):
# Reference: [the generated image]. Modify the image to {your change}.
# Preserve {anchors}. Change {target}.
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't use Midjourney-style flag syntax**. Nano Banana ignores `--ar`, expects `aspectRatio` parameter

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't expect Midjourney-level aesthetic by default**. Nano Banana is a workhorse, not a stylist. Stack mood adjectives explicitly
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't pile multiple modifications in one image-to-image prompt**, one change per pass produces cleaner results

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't forget the "preserve" clause in image-to-image**, without it, Nano Banana treats the reference as loose inspiration and drifts
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't include text content in image prompts**, composite separately; text rendering is mediocre

[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › API access] Through Google Gemini API (`gemini-2.5-flash-image` model endpoint). Available via:
Gemini API direct; Vertex AI; Replicate; fal.ai (under "google/nano-banana")
[Adapter: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) › API access] Same prompt syntax across all four.

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot)] Seedance 2.0 is the multi-shot model. It can generate a **short sequence of cuts in a single generation** while holding subject and environment consistency across them. Reach for it when several consecutive storyboard beats share one subject and you want them to feel like one continuous take, it beats stitching four independent Kling clips that drift apart. For a single isolated shot, Kling is the simpler default.

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot)] With video the **camera motion is load-bearing**, and with Seedance the **cut structure is also load-bearing**, you describe the sequence of shots, not just one frame.

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Syntax pattern] Single shot:
{Camera motion sentence, leading.} {Subject and action.} {Environment and lighting from series_lock.} {Color grade and mood from brand_lock.}

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Syntax pattern] Multi-shot sequence (Seedance's strength):
Shot 1: {camera + action}. Shot 2: {camera + action}. Shot 3: {camera + action}. Consistent subject throughout: {series_lock character anchor, verbatim}. {Environment and lighting from series_lock.} {Color grade and mood from brand_lock.}
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Parameters] Parameter: `duration` · Default: `5s` per shot block · Notes: Multi-shot sequences run longer; check the current fal.ai ceiling
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Parameters] Parameter: `start_image` · Default: optional · Notes: Image-to-video reference for the opening frame
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Parameters] Parameter: `shots` · Default: 1 · Notes: Number of cuts in the sequence when using multi-shot mode

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Parameters] # shot_02-shot_04. Seedance 2.0: ar=9:16, shots=3, multi-shot sequence
{prompt}
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Length] Seedance handles **80–150 words**. In multi-shot mode, keep each shot clause short, one camera move and one action per cut.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › When to use multi-shot vs single] Situation: One beat, one frame · Mode: Single shot (or use Kling)
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › When to use multi-shot vs single] Situation: 2–4 consecutive beats, same subject, want continuity · Mode: Multi-shot sequence
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › When to use multi-shot vs single] Situation: Beats with different subjects/locations · Mode: Separate generations, assemble in edit

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › When to use multi-shot vs single] Map consecutive `shots.json` entries that share a subject into one Seedance multi-shot prompt; reference them by id range in the comment.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Motion vocabulary] The shot grammar `motion` field maps directly. One move per cut.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Example] **Three consecutive beats of the same founder, mapped to one sequence.**

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Example] Shot 1: static eye-level, the founder closes his laptop and exhales. Shot 2: slow push toward his face as he looks toward the window. Shot 3: handheld over-the-shoulder as he stands and crosses the room. Consistent subject throughout: a founder in his mid-thirties with salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck. Minimalist home office, white walls, oak desk, soft natural side-light from a large window on the left, warm afternoon golden hour. Warm filmic color grade with muted teal shadows. Calm, considered, operator mood.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't force unrelated beats into one sequence.** Multi-shot is for shots that genuinely belong to one take.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't write more than ~4 cuts per generation.** Consistency degrades past that; split and assemble in edit.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't vary the character anchor between cuts.** Restate it once for the whole sequence, verbatim.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't include text content.** Composite captions from `text-overlays.json` in post.
[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't stack two camera moves inside one cut.** One move per cut.

[Adapter: Seedance 2.0 (motion-aware video, multi-shot) › Output handoff] Seedance returns a sequence as a single clip (or a small set). It still needs: editorial trimming to exact storyboard timing, text-overlay compositing, a color-grade pass, and audio. Multi-shot output usually needs *less* assembly than stitched single clips, which is the point. Say so in handoff.

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0)] ByteDance's Seedream models are the high-volume cost-efficient choice. Quality is below Flux 2 Pro and Midjourney v7 but above older mid-tier models, and the cost-per-image is roughly 5–10× lower. Choose Seedream when you're producing **many variations or doing rapid concept iteration**, not for hero/final assets.

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0)] For storyboard work, Seedream is useful for the storyboard preview pass: render every shot quickly to validate composition before committing to higher-cost generation for finals.

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Syntax pattern] Seedream rewards **short, precise prompts**. Long descriptive prompts underperform, the model interprets them as competing weights and produces mush. Closer to Midjourney's style than Flux's.
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Syntax pattern] {Subject phrase}, {action}, {environment}, {lighting}, {mood/style}, {aspect note}
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Syntax pattern] Comma-separated, no full sentences.
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Parameters] Seedream is API-driven through fal.ai, Replicate, or BytePlus direct:
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Parameters] Parameter: `seed` · Default: per-storyboard · Notes: Critical for series consistency
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Parameters] Parameter: `guidance_scale` · Default: `4.5` · Notes: Lower = more creative, higher = more literal
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Parameters] Parameter: `steps` · Default: `28` · Notes: Default. Increase to 50 for higher quality at cost
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Length] **40–70 words per prompt**. Shorter than most. Don't pad.

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Composition pattern] {Framing} of {character anchor}, {action}, {environment from series_lock}, {lighting from series_lock}, {color grade from brand_lock}, {one mood adjective}, photorealistic

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Example] **Output prompt:**
Medium shot of founder mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, leaning forward at laptop, face turned to window light, minimalist home office, oak desk, soft natural side-light from large window, warm afternoon, warm filmic color grade, muted teal shadows, calm operator mood, photorealistic
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the right choice] - **Storyboard preview pass**, render all shots quickly at low cost to validate composition before final pass
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the right choice] - **High-volume social content**, when you need 50+ images per day and the quality bar allows it
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the right choice] - **Concept exploration**, quick iteration on shot ideas before committing to a final generator
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the right choice] - **Placeholder content**, assets that will be replaced once the brand-lock is finalized
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the wrong choice] - **Hero shots / final deliverables**. Flux 2 Pro or Midjourney v7 produce noticeably better output
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the wrong choice] - **Photorealistic product shots**. Flux is meaningfully better for product fidelity
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the wrong choice] - **Text-heavy designs**. Ideogram or GPT Image
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › When Seedream is the wrong choice] - **Cinematic mood pieces**. Midjourney is the move

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Series consistency] Seedream's character consistency is weaker than Midjourney `--cref` or Ideogram omni-reference. To compensate:
- **Lock the seed** at the storyboard level (same seed across all shots in a series)
- **Verbatim repeat** the character anchor string from series_lock in every prompt
- **Don't vary** the lighting language between shots, series_lock string in, no paraphrasing
- **Accept** that some shots will need re-rolls; budget for it
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't write paragraphs**. Seedream wants comma-separated phrases
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't use `--ar` syntax**, pass aspect_ratio as a parameter
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't include text content**, text rendering is poor; composite separately
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't expect Midjourney aesthetic**. Seedream produces clean but less art-directed output
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't skip the seed lock for series work**, without it, character consistency breaks

[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › API access] **fal.ai**, `bytedance/seedream-4.5` and `bytedance/seedream-4.0`; **Replicate**, `bytedance/seedream-4.5`; **BytePlus**, direct API, requires their account
[Adapter: Seedream (4.5 / 4.0) › API access] Same prompt syntax across surfaces.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio)] Veo 3 is the dialogue and lipsync model. It is the only adapter that generates **synchronised native audio**, speech, ambience, and sound effects, in the same pass as the video. It also has the strongest prompt adherence and physical realism of the four motion models. It is the most expensive, so reserve it for shots that actually need spoken dialogue, lipsync, or audio baked in. For silent B-roll and camera moves, Kling is the cheaper default.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio)] With video the **camera motion is load-bearing**. When the shot has dialogue, the **spoken line is also load-bearing** and is written into the prompt (this is the one place where text belongs in a prompt, it is audio, not on-screen text).

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Syntax pattern] {Camera motion sentence, leading.} {Subject and action over the duration.} {Dialogue line, in quotes, if any.} {Environment and lighting from series_lock.} {Audio direction.} {Color grade and mood from brand_lock.}
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Parameters] Parameter: `duration` · Default: `8s` · Notes: Veo's native clip length
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Parameters] Parameter: `generate_audio` · Default: `true` · Notes: The reason to choose Veo. Set `false` only for silent shots

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Parameters] # shot_04. Veo 3: duration=8s, ar=9:16, generate_audio=true
{prompt}
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Length] Veo handles **80–150 words**. Spend the headroom on action timing and audio direction, not adjective stacks.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Dialogue and lipsync] When the shot calls for the subject to speak, put the exact line in quotes:
The founder looks directly into the lens and says, "I built the system once, and it runs without me."

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Dialogue and lipsync] Keep spoken lines to what fits the duration, roughly 12–18 words for an 8s clip. Direct the delivery ("calm, unhurried"). Veo lipsyncs the quoted line.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Audio direction] Even on silent shots Veo can place ambience. Be explicit and brief:
- "Audio: quiet room tone, faint keyboard, no music."
- "Audio: soft afternoon ambience, distant street."

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Audio direction] If the brand-lock or storyboard owns the audio bed (VO recorded separately, music added in post), set `generate_audio=false` and skip this section so Veo does not invent a competing track.
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Example] **Shot with `motion = "static"` and a spoken line.**

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Example] Static camera, locked off, eye level. A founder in his mid-thirties with salt-and-pepper hair in a navy crewneck sits at his laptop in a minimalist home office and looks directly into the lens. He says, "I built the system once, and it runs without me," calm and unhurried. Soft natural side-light from a large window on the left, warm afternoon golden hour. Audio: quiet room tone, faint keyboard, no music. Warm filmic color grade with muted teal shadows. Calm, considered, operator mood.
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't use Veo for silent B-roll.** You are paying for an audio engine you turned off; use Kling.
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't overrun the duration with dialogue.** A line that needs 12s of speech will clip or rush at 8s.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't put on-screen text in the prompt.** Spoken lines are fine; rendered captions still come from `text-overlays.json` in post.
[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Pitfalls to avoid] - **Don't let Veo's auto-audio fight a post audio bed.** Pick one owner of sound per shot.

[Adapter: Veo 3 (motion-aware video, native audio) › Output handoff] Veo clips arrive with audio attached. They still need: editorial assembly to timing, on-screen text compositing from `text-overlays.json`, a color-grade pass, and an audio decision, keep Veo's native track, or mute it and use the storyboard's recorded VO and music. State which in handoff.

[Consistency Locks] Visual consistency across a storyboard is the hardest problem in AI image generation. Generators are stateless, every prompt is interpreted fresh. Without consistency locks, shot 1 and shot 7 will look like different productions.
[Consistency Locks] This document covers the techniques that actually work in 2026.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 1. Verbatim character anchors] The most effective single technique. The character is described in `series_lock.character` once, and that exact string appears in every shot's prompt verbatim. No paraphrasing, no synonyms, no "improvement."

[Consistency Locks › Lock 1. Verbatim character anchors] **Good (consistent):**
shot_01: "founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, stubble"
shot_02: "founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, stubble"
shot_07: "founder, mid-thirties, salt-and-pepper hair, navy crewneck, stubble"

[Consistency Locks › Lock 1. Verbatim character anchors] **Bad (inconsistent):**
shot_01: "a thoughtful entrepreneur in his thirties, dark hair, casual sweater"
shot_02: "founder, 35 years old, salt-pepper hair, blue knit top"
shot_07: "the man in the home office, navy shirt"
[Consistency Locks › Lock 1. Verbatim character anchors] Even small variations compound. Lock the string. Repeat verbatim.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 2. Verbatim environment anchors] Same principle for `series_lock.environment`. The environment string is identical in every shot prompt. The shot's individual subject describes what changes within the environment, not the environment itself.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 3. Verbatim lighting anchors] Same principle for `series_lock.lighting`. Lighting direction in particular is critical, flipping window-left to window-right between shots produces obvious cuts where there shouldn't be any.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 4. Seed locking] For generators that support seeds (Flux, Seedream, Ideogram, Stable Diffusion), set the seed at the storyboard level. Same seed across every shot. This anchors the generator's randomness so character features carry.
[Consistency Locks › Lock 4. Seed locking] The adapter reads this and applies to every prompt.
[Consistency Locks › Lock 4. Seed locking] **Caveat:** Midjourney and some motion models (Veo, Seedance) handle seeds differently, or not at all. Document seed-locking as best-effort, not guaranteed.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] For Midjourney v7, Ideogram v3, and Nano Banana, you can pass a reference image alongside the prompt to anchor character or style.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] **Workflow:**
1. Generate the hero shot first (any shot, usually `shot_01` or whichever is most defining)
2. Use that image as the reference for every subsequent shot
3. Each subsequent prompt has the verbatim character anchor PLUS the reference image link
[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] For Midjourney: `--cref {url} --cw 50` (character weight 50 = features only, not clothing).
[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] For Ideogram: `omni-reference` parameter with the image.
[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] For Nano Banana: `referenceImages` array.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 5. Reference images (`--cref`, omni-reference, image-to-image)] **This is the most effective lock for character consistency** in 2026. Use it whenever the storyboard features the same person across multiple shots.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 6. Style references] When the storyboard has a distinctive visual style (specific film stock, specific lighting school, specific color theory), use a style reference image:
- Midjourney: `--sref {url}`
- Ideogram: style reference parameter
- Flux: not directly supported; bake style language into prompt instead
[Consistency Locks › Lock 6. Style references] A consistent style reference across all shots produces aesthetic continuity even when characters or environments shift.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 7. Lighting direction continuity] A subtle one that breaks scenes when violated. If `series_lock.lighting` says "soft natural side-light, large window LEFT", then every shot's lighting must respect that direction.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 7. Lighting direction continuity] When a shot reverses character orientation (e.g., over-the-shoulder reverse), update the rationale to acknowledge the lighting flip:
"rationale": "OTS reverse, light source now camera-right (matching scene continuity from window-left in master)"
[Consistency Locks › Lock 7. Lighting direction continuity] If you find yourself flipping light direction without rationale, you're producing visual jump cuts.

[Consistency Locks › Lock 8. Color grade flow-through] The `series_lock.color_grade` string flows into every prompt verbatim. Same as character/environment/lighting. If shot 1 is "warm filmic, muted teal shadows" and shot 7 is "cinematic teal and orange", the audience will read it as different scenes.
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Character · Failure mode: Different person every shot
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Environment · Failure mode: Scene jumps
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Lighting · Failure mode: Time-of-day jumps, eye-line breaks
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Seed · Failure mode: Random feature drift
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Reference image · Failure mode: Loose character interpretation
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Missing lock: Color grade · Failure mode: Tonal whiplash
[Consistency Locks › Failure modes when locks are missing] Every one of these is a production problem editorial cannot fully fix. Lock at the prompt level. Save the editor's time.

[Consistency Locks › What doesn't work] A few things people try that don't actually fix consistency:
- **Adding "consistent character" or "same person" to the prompt**, generators don't read meta-instructions
- **Numbering shots in the prompt** ("shot 3 of 7, same as before"), generators don't have memory across calls
- **Long descriptive paragraphs of the character**, past 4–5 features, the generator starts dropping details randomly
- **Asking for "exactly the same"**, there is no such thing in stateless image gen; you reduce drift, you don't eliminate it
[Consistency Locks › What doesn't work] Accept that some shots will need re-rolls. Budget for it. The locks reduce the failure rate; they don't eliminate it.
[Failure Modes] What goes wrong when generated images don't match the storyboard, and what to fix at the prompt level vs. accept as editorial work.

[Failure Modes › Failure 1. The "AI look"] **Symptoms:** plastic skin, oversaturated colors, eyes too symmetrical, hands wrong, generic stock-photo composition, lighting that's too even, "rendered" feel.
**Causes:**
Generic mood adjectives ("beautiful", "stunning", "amazing"); Stable Diffusion crutches ("4k", "highly detailed", "masterpiece") in non-SD generators; Missing photographic specifics; No "never" list applied from brand-lock

[Failure Modes › Failure 1. The "AI look"] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Add specific lens and aperture ("50mm prime, f/2.0")
- Add film stock or camera reference ("Sony FX6", "Kodak Portra 400 film stock")
- Add "natural skin texture, no AI rendering artifacts" closing line (Flux, GPT Image)
- Verify brand-lock "never" list is being applied, if it includes "no AI uncanny", surface that into the prompt
- Use Flux 2 Pro or Midjourney v7 instead of cheaper models for hero shots
[Failure Modes › Failure 1. The "AI look"] **Accept editorially when:** the brief is for stylized content where realism isn't the goal.

[Failure Modes › Failure 2. Character drift across shots] **Symptoms:** same person looks different in shot 1 vs shot 5; clothing changes; hair color shifts; age perceived differently.
**Causes:**
- Series_lock character string paraphrased rather than verbatim
- No reference image passed (`--cref`, omni-reference)
- Seed not locked
- Too few features described in character anchor (gives generator too much room)

[Failure Modes › Failure 2. Character drift across shots] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Verify character string is verbatim across every prompt
- Add 1–2 more specific features ("small scar above left eyebrow", "black wireframe glasses")
- Use reference image after the first successful shot
- Lock seed at storyboard level
- For Midjourney, use `--cref` with `--cw 50`
[Failure Modes › Failure 2. Character drift across shots] **Accept editorially when:** character consistency is genuinely impossible to lock. Budget re-rolls, typically 2–3× per problematic shot.

[Failure Modes › Failure 3. Text in image looks bad] **Symptoms:** text is misspelled, kerning is off, font is wrong, multiple text elements compete.
**Causes:**
- Text was put in the image prompt instead of being composited
- Wrong generator chosen (using Midjourney for text-heavy work)
- Multiple text elements in one prompt

[Failure Modes › Failure 3. Text in image looks bad] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- The right answer is almost always: **don't put text in the prompt**. Composite separately from `text-overlays.json`.
- If text must be in-image (poster work), use Ideogram v3 with explicit override flag
- Limit to one text element per prompt
- Use simple fonts (sans-serif, clean serif), cursive and decorative fonts fail even on Ideogram
[Failure Modes › Failure 3. Text in image looks bad] **Accept editorially when:** the deliverable genuinely requires baked-in text and Ideogram's output is close enough to retouch.

[Failure Modes › Failure 4. Lighting direction inconsistency] **Symptoms:** shot 3 has light from window-left, shot 4 has light from window-right, they cut together as a continuity error.
**Causes:**
- Lighting language paraphrased rather than verbatim from series_lock
- Reverse-angle shots not flagged in rationale
- Generator interpreting lighting ambiguously

[Failure Modes › Failure 4. Lighting direction inconsistency] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Verify lighting string is verbatim across prompts
- Be explicit about direction: "from camera-left" not "from one side"
- For reverse-angle shots, flag in rationale and update lighting language for that shot only
- For Flux and GPT Image, add the photographic spec ("key light camera-left at 45 degrees")
[Failure Modes › Failure 4. Lighting direction inconsistency] **Accept editorially when:** lighting drift is subtle enough that color grading will fix it.

[Failure Modes › Failure 5. Composition doesn't reserve space for text overlay] **Symptoms:** the storyboard says text goes in the right third, but the generated image has the subject filling the right third.
**Causes:**
Shot subject didn't include negative-space note; Generator interpreting "centered subject" by default

[Failure Modes › Failure 5. Composition doesn't reserve space for text overlay] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Add explicit composition note: "subject framed in left third, right two-thirds open for text overlay"
- For GPT Image (best at spatial reasoning), use percentage references: "subject at left 30% of frame"
- Re-roll with explicit composition prompt, this often fixes on second try
[Failure Modes › Failure 5. Composition doesn't reserve space for text overlay] **Accept editorially when:** image is otherwise great. Reposition text overlay to fit the actual composition.

[Failure Modes › Failure 6. Series feels "different" even with locks applied] **Symptoms:** all locks are in place, prompts look right, but the storyboard feels disjointed when viewed end-to-end.
**Causes:**
- Color grade language drifting between shots (one says "warm filmic", another says "cinematic")
- Aspect ratio drift (some 9:16 generations are taller than others)
- Mood adjectives shifting ("calm" in shot 1 vs "energetic" in shot 5 even though brief was uniform)

[Failure Modes › Failure 6. Series feels "different" even with locks applied] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Audit every prompt against series_lock and brand-lock, verbatim check
- Verify aspect ratio is identical across all prompts
- Lock the brand mood adjectives, same set in every prompt

[Failure Modes › Failure 6. Series feels "different" even with locks applied] **Accept editorially when:** the disjoint feel is below the noise floor for the medium (e.g. fast-cut social where each shot is on screen <2s).

[Failure Modes › Failure 7, "Looks fine but doesn't match the brief"] **Symptoms:** image is technically good but doesn't capture what the brief was actually about.
**Causes:**
- The shot subject in `shots.json` was vague
- The brief context wasn't surfaced into the prompt
- The generator is producing competent generic output rather than specific intent

[Failure Modes › Failure 7, "Looks fine but doesn't match the brief"] **Prompt-level fixes:**
- Tighten the shot's subject field, what specifically is the audience meant to feel or notice
- Include a one-phrase intent at the end ("the moment of recognition", "the calm before the decision")
- For complex scenes, add a "what this shot conveys" line

[Failure Modes › Failure 7, "Looks fine but doesn't match the brief"] **Accept editorially when:** generation is close enough that retouching gets there. Don't burn API credits chasing perfect on-prompt.

[Failure Modes › When to stop iterating prompts] Three signs:
1. You've re-rolled the same shot 5+ times with no improvement → the prompt is fine; the model can't render this concept; pick a different shot or different generator
2. You're tweaking single words and hoping → you've hit prompt-level diminishing returns; move to image-to-image refinement (Nano Banana) or post-production
3. The image is 80% right and the gap is editorial → ship to post and let the editor finish
[Failure Modes › When to stop iterating prompts] Generation is one stage in a pipeline. Don't try to make it the whole pipeline.

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers] Every image prompt this skill produces is composed from five layers. Four are inputs, one is applied at compose-time. Understanding the layers is the difference between bulletproof prompts and lottery tickets.

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 1. Brand Lock] **What:** the locked brand parameters for the entire project.
**Source:** `brand-lock.snapshot.md` referenced in `shots.json`.
**Constant across:** every storyboard, every shot.

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 1. Brand Lock] Contains:
- Palette (hex values)
- Typography (font names, weights)
- Mood descriptors (3–5 adjectives that describe the brand's emotional posture)
- "Never" list (things this brand never does, e.g. "no stock photo aesthetic", "no AI uncanny", "no over-saturated", "no shouting copy")
- Aspect ratios used
- Color grade direction
[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 1. Brand Lock] This layer answers: **what does the brand always look and feel like?**

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 2. Series Lock] **What:** the locked anchors for this specific storyboard.
**Source:** `shots.json` → `series_lock`.
**Constant across:** every shot in this one storyboard.

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 2. Series Lock] Contains:
- Character anchor (who's in frame, described identically every shot)
- Environment description (where the action takes place, identical every shot)
- Lighting setup (direction, source, color temperature, identical every shot)
- Color grade (filmic look, identical every shot)
[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 2. Series Lock] This layer answers: **what stays the same across this storyboard?**
[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 2. Series Lock] The series_lock is what makes shot 1 and shot 7 feel like the same piece. Without it, every generated frame looks like a different production.

[Prompt Anatomy: The Five Layers › Layer 3. Shot Spec] **What:** the per-shot variables.
**Source:** `shots.json` → `shots[i]`.
**Variable across:** every shot.
